title: Operators
summary: Operators let you calculate, compare values, and combine decisions.

subtopics.title: Math
subtopics.explanation: Arithmetic operators include `+`, `-`, `*`, and `/`. They add, subtract, multiply, and divide numeric values. JavaScript also uses `+` to join strings, so convert form values before doing arithmetic. Parentheses make the intended order clear, especially when an expression has several steps. Parentheses document the intended calculation order. If user input begins as text, conversion and validation should happen before arithmetic. Arithmetic operators are like calculator keys that perform one calculation.

subtopics.title: Comparisons
subtopics.explanation: Comparison operators such as `===`, `<`, and `>=` compare values and produce a boolean. Use them in conditions, and do not confuse comparison with assignment: `=` assigns a value. For example, `count === 0` checks whether the count is zero. Comparisons return booleans that can control an if or filter. Be careful when comparing values with different types because coercion can obscure intent. A comparison is like asking a yes-or-no question about two values.

subtopics.title: Strict equality
subtopics.explanation: Strict equality `===` compares without converting values of different types first. Therefore, `5 === "5"` is false. Use it for predictable checks, such as comparing an ID string to a known ID. If values come from an input, convert and validate them before comparison. Strict equality does not convert text into a number. Convert at the boundary when the same identifier can arrive in more than one representation. It is like checking both a package’s label and contents before deciding two packages match.

subtopics.title: Logical operators
subtopics.explanation: `&&` means both conditions must be true; `||` means at least one may be true. For example, require both `isSignedIn` and `hasPermission` before showing a protected action. JavaScript short-circuits these operators, so later expressions may not run when the result is already determined. Logical operators short-circuit: the right side may not run. This can guard an optional action, but avoid hiding required work inside a condition. Logical AND is like needing two keys; OR accepts either key.

subtopics.title: Negation
subtopics.explanation: `!` negates a value’s truthiness and returns a boolean. `!isReady` is true when `isReady` is false. Use negation sparingly and name booleans positively when that makes a condition easier to read. Repeated `!` operators often hide the real decision. Negation works best with a clear positive boolean name. For compound conditions, state what is true rather than stacking negations. Negation is like flipping a yes-or-no switch.

foundations.overview: Operators combine values or compare them. Arithmetic operators calculate; comparison operators produce true or false; logical operators combine conditions. Think of operators as small instructions between values. Understand the result each operator produces, and use strict equality so JavaScript does not silently convert different types when comparing them.
foundations.whyItMatters: Operator behavior influences calculations and control flow throughout a program. Explicit comparisons and named conditions reduce mistakes caused by coercion or unreadable logic.
foundations.browserPerspective: The JavaScript engine parses your expression into a tree based on precedence and associativity, then evaluates nodes bottom-up. Short-circuiting means the engine may skip evaluating the right operand of && or || entirely, which is both a performance and correctness feature.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Setting defaults (name ?? 'Guest'), guarding access (user?.address?.city), conditional rendering (isLoading ? <Spinner/> : <List/>), validation (age >= 18 && hasConsent), and counters (i++) all lean on operators every single day.
foundations.businessImpact: Correct operator use prevents crashes from missing data and wrong-default bugs (like treating a valid 0 as missing), which directly affects whether features behave correctly for real users.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Choosing === over ==, ?? over ||, and ?. for safe access removes whole categories of subtle bugs and makes code intent obvious to teammates and reviewers.
foundations.performanceImpact: Operators themselves are extremely fast, but short-circuiting lets you skip expensive right-hand evaluations (e.g., cache && computeExpensive()), which is the main performance lever in this topic.
commonUseCases: Safely reading nested data with optional chaining ?.
Conditional values and rendering with the ternary operator
Validate a number submitted through a form.
Decide whether a user can access a protected control.

commonMisconceptions.myth: == and === do the same thing, == is just shorter.
commonMisconceptions.reality: == converts types before comparing, producing surprising results like 0 == '' being true; === compares value and type with no conversion.
|| replaces any falsy value (including 0, '', false), while ?? only replaces null and undefined — a critical difference when 0 or '' are valid.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A single equals sign compares two values.
commonMisconceptions.reality: A single `=` assigns; use comparison operators such as `===` to test equality.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Logical operators always return true or false.
commonMisconceptions.reality: JavaScript `&&` and `||` return operand values and short-circuit, which matters in expressions.

visualExplorer.title: How an expression with mixed operators is evaluated
visualExplorer.caption: Step through how JavaScript applies precedence and short-circuiting to resolve a compound expression.

config.intro: Follow how `const result = a ?? b || c && d` is parsed and evaluated step by step.

steps.name: Parse by precedence
steps.detail: The engine builds an expression tree: && binds tighter than ||, and ?? cannot mix with them without parentheses, so structure is determined before any value is computed.

steps.name: Evaluate left operand
steps.detail: Evaluation starts from the leftmost operand, resolving each value as the tree is walked from the bottom up.

steps.name: Apply short-circuiting
steps.detail: If an && hits a falsy operand or an || hits a truthy operand, the remaining operand on that side is skipped entirely.

steps.name: Resolve nullish vs falsy
steps.detail: ?? only falls back on null/undefined, while || falls back on any falsy value — so the same input can take different branches.

steps.name: Return the operand
steps.detail: Logical operators return one of the original operands (not a boolean), and that value is assigned to result.

interactiveExamples.title: Strict vs loose equality
interactiveExamples.explanation: === compares value and type; == coerces first. Watch how the same comparison flips between them.

sandbox.code:
console.log(1 === '1'); // false — number vs string
console.log(1 == '1');  // true  — '1' coerced to 1
console.log(0 == false); // true  — both become 0
console.log(0 === false); // false — number vs boolean
console.log(null == undefined); // true
console.log(null === undefined); // false

interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: false, true, true, false, true, false.

interactiveExamples.title: ?? and ?. for safe defaults and access
interactiveExamples.explanation: Nullish coalescing keeps a valid 0, and optional chaining avoids a crash on missing nested data.

sandbox.code:
const settings = { volume: 0, profile: null };

console.log(settings.volume || 5); // 5 — wrong! 0 treated as missing
console.log(settings.volume ?? 5); // 0 — correct, 0 is a real value

console.log(settings.profile?.name); // undefined — no crash
console.log(settings.profile?.name ?? 'Anonymous'); // 'Anonymous'

codeLab.title: Build a safe config reader
codeLab.instructions: Implement getSetting(config, key, fallback) that returns config[key] if it exists, but uses fallback ONLY when the value is null or undefined (a value of 0 or '' should be kept). Use optional chaining and nullish coalescing.
hints: Use config?.[key] so a null config doesn't throw.
Use ?? (not ||) so a valid 0 isn't replaced by the fallback.

keyTakeaways: Comparison operators such as `===`, `<`, and `>=` compare values and produce a boolean.
Strict equality `===` compares without converting values of different types first.
`&&` means both conditions must be true; `||` means at least one may be true.
`!` negates a value’s truthiness and returns a boolean.
